<reason>Both sides were sharp and disciplined, but PRO (B) repeatedly forced CON onto weaker ground. B turned CON's own opening line ("the giants already run cash infrastructure") into a cost concession, exposed the prepaid-card alternative as circular (bought with cash at a retailer), and answered the interchange point so cashless was no longer "free." CON's dichotomy ("benefit tiny or cost real") was met honestly by B conceding "small and real" costs and reframing the mandate as a floor judged on its worst day, with the fire-exit analogy. Most damaging, CON's A2 answer — yes, tender could buy bread nowhere, but "a targeted rule would follow" — let B recast CON as merely opposing the timing of the mandate, and B pointed out the tension between CON arguing at length that rational retailers drop cash and then promising they never will. CON's insurance-frame closing was clean and had the last word, and CON's networked-till point was a reasonable attack on resilience, but B's processor-outage-vs-blackout distinction was more plausible and never squarely answered. B's two clipped turns are an execution cost and keep this competitive rather than solid, but B made the debate easier to decide.</reason>
<best_rebuttal>B's dismantling of the prepaid card ([B2.6]-[B2.8]): "CON's alternative to cash acceptance depends on cash acceptance," plus the fee "poverty surcharge," forced CON to pivot to SNAP/EBT — which B's Q1 then hit with the woman who "qualifies for no benefits," leaving CON's answer resting on the status quo that "nearly all" retailers still take cash.</best_rebuttal>
